source_text: Attoniti ergo, quid contra me scripserit, audiamus. Verba - inquit - de libro meo tibi a me misso tibique notissimo ista posuit, quae refutare conatus est: "damnatores nos esse nuptiarum, operisque divini, quo ex maribus et feminis Deus homines creat, invidiosissime clamitant; quoniam dicimus, eos qui de tali commixtione nascuntur, trahere originale peccatum; eosque, de qualibuscumque parentibus nascantur, non negamus adhuc esse sub diabolo, nisi renascantur in Christo " [n15] . In his verbis meis testimonium Apostoli, quod interposui praetermisit, cuius se premi magna mole sentiebat. Ego enim cum dixissem, homines trahere originale peccatum, mox adiunxi: De quo Apostolus ait: "r unum hominem peccatum intravit in mundum, et per peccatum mors; et ita in omnes homines pertransiit, in quo omnes peccaverunt " [n16] ; quo testimonio, ut diximus, praetermisso, cetera illa contexuit quae supra commemorata sunt. Novit enim quemadmodum soleant haec verba apostolica, quae praetermisit, accipere catholicorum corda fidelium; quae verba tam recta et tanta luce fulgentia, tenebrosis et tortuosis interpretationibus novi haeretici obscurare et depravare moliuntur. Deinde alia mea verba subtexuit, ubi dixi: "c advertunt, quod ita nuptiarum bonum malo originali quod inde trahitur non potest accusari, sicut adulteriorum et fornicationum malum bono naturali, quod inde nascitur, non potest excusari. Nam, sicut peccatum, sive hinc sive inde a parvulis trahatur, opus est diaboli, sic homo, sive hinc sive inde nascatur, opus est Dei ". Etiam hic ea praetermisit, in quibus aures catholicas timuit. Nam ut ad haec verba veniretur, supra dictum erat a nobis: "c ergo quia dicimus, quod antiquissima atque firmissima catholicae fidei regula continetur, isti novelli et perversi dogmatis assertores, qui nihil peccati esse in parvulis dicunt quod lavacro regenerationis abluatur, tamquam damnemus nuptias, et tamquam opus Dei, hoc est hominem qui ex illis nascitur, opus diaboli esse dicamus, infideliter vel imperite calumniantur " [n17] . His ergo nostris praetermissis sequuntur illa nostra quae posuit, sicut supra scriptum est [n18] . Quousque simplicitati, qui haec loqueris, religiosorum pectorum et imperitis auribus perstabis illudere? Quem ad finem sese impudentia effrenata iactabit? Nihil te, cum haec scriberes, censura doctorum virorum, nihil reverentia futuri iudicii, nihil ipsa litterarum monumenta moverunt? Patere iam fallaciam tuam, et deprehensam teneri non vides? Quid in primo, quid in secundo opere conscripseris, quem nostrum ignorare arbitraris? Libuit enim prorsus, et decuit, his te compellare modis, quibus in parricidam publicum eloquens consul infremuit [n19] .
pass_a_gloss: Astonished therefore, let us hear what he has written against me. 'Words,' he says, 'from my book sent by me to you and very well known to you he placed these, which he tried to refute: "they cry out most invidiously that we are condemners of marriages and of the divine work by which God creates humans from males and females; because we say that those who are born from such a mingling draw original sin; and we do not deny that they, from whatever parents they are born, are still under the devil, unless they are reborn in Christ." In these words of mine he passed over the testimony of the Apostle which I inserted, by whose great mass he felt himself pressed. For when I had said that humans draw original sin, I at once joined: Of which the Apostle says: "Through one human sin entered into the world, and through sin death; and so it passed through unto all humans, in whom all sinned"; which testimony, as we have said, having been passed over, he wove together those other things which have been recalled above. For he knows how the hearts of faithful catholics are accustomed to receive these apostolic words which he passed over; which words, so straight and shining with so great a light, the new heretics strive to darken and deprave by gloomy and twisted interpretations. Then he wove under other words of mine, where I said: "They do not notice that thus the good of marriages cannot be accused by the original evil which is drawn from there, just as the evil of adulteries and fornications cannot be excused by the natural good which is born from there. For, just as sin, whether it is drawn by little ones from this side or from that, is a work of the devil, so a human, whether born from this side or from that, is a work of God." Here too he passed over those things in which he feared catholic ears. For that these words might be reached, it had been said above by us: "Because therefore we say that which is contained in the most ancient and most firm rule of the catholic faith, these asserters of a novel and perverse dogma, who say there is no sin in little ones which may be washed away by the bath of regeneration, as though we condemn marriages, and as though we say that the work of God, that is the human who is born from them, is a work of the devil, slander faithlessly or unskillfully." These things of ours therefore having been passed over, there follow those things of ours which he placed, as has been written above.' How far, you who speak these things, will you persist in mocking the simplicity of religious breasts and unskilled ears? To what end will unbridled shamelessness fling itself? Did nothing, when you were writing these things, the censure of learned men, nothing the reverence of the coming judgment, nothing the very monuments of letters move you? Do you not see your deceit now lie open, and be held caught? What you wrote in the first work, what in the second, which of us do you think does not know? For it has pleased outright, and it was fitting, to address you in these modes with which the eloquent consul roared against a public parricide.

pass_b_english: Let us listen, then, in astonishment to what he has written against me. He says: 'He quoted these words from the book I sent you, which you know very well, and attempted to refute them: “They shout with the utmost malice that we condemn marriage and God's work, by which God creates human beings from males and females, because we say that those born from such a union inherit original sin. We do not deny that, whatever parents they are born from, they remain under the devil unless they are reborn in Christ (compare John 3:3–5)” (Titus 3:5)' (Augustine, On Marriage and Concupiscence 2.2). Augustine continues: 'From these words of mine he omitted the apostle's testimony that I had inserted, because he felt himself crushed by its great weight. For when I said that human beings inherit original sin, I immediately added: “Of this the apostle says, Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death; and so it passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Romans 5:12) (John 3:3–5). After omitting that testimony, as we have said, he joined together the other statements mentioned above. He knows how the hearts of faithful catholics commonly receive these apostolic words that he omitted, words so straightforward and shining with such light, which new heretics try to obscure and distort through dark and twisted interpretations. He then appended other words of mine where I said: “They do not notice that the good of marriage cannot be blamed because of the original evil inherited from it, just as the evil of adultery and fornication cannot be excused because of the natural good born from them. For just as sin, whether infants inherit it from the one source or the other, is the devil's work, so a human being, whether born from the one or the other, is God's work.” Here too he omitted what he feared catholic ears would hear. Before arriving at these words, we had said: “Because we say this, which is contained in the most ancient and firmly established rule of the catholic faith, these advocates of a new and perverse doctrine, who say that there is no sin in infants to be washed away in the bath of rebirth (compare Titus 3:5), slander us faithlessly or ignorantly, as though we condemned marriage and called God's work, the human being born from it, the devil's work” (Augustine, On Marriage and Concupiscence 1.1). After these omitted words of ours come those of ours that he quoted, as written above' (Augustine, On Marriage and Concupiscence 2.3–4). How long will you who say these things persist in mocking the simplicity of devout hearts and uneducated ears? How far will your unbridled shamelessness flaunt itself? When you wrote this, were you not moved at all by the judgment of learned men, by reverence for the coming judgment, or by the written records themselves? Do you not see that your deceit already lies exposed, caught and held fast? Which of us do you suppose does not know what you wrote in your first and second works? I have deliberately chosen, and rightly chosen, to address you in the terms in which the eloquent consul thundered against a traitor to his country (Cicero, Against Catiline 1.1).

choices.why: Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

variants.reading: The source has damaged word openings in Augustine's embedded quotation: “r unum”, “c advertunt”, and “c ergo”. These have been restored from the quoted passage and context as “Through one”, “They do not notice”, and “Because ... this”. Romans 5:12 preserves the Latin “in whom”, central to the dispute, rather than replacing it with a modern Bible's interpretive rendering.
